extracted.intended_audience: young British men and women seeking guidance in polite conversation and conduct (early-18th-century society)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical rules and moral advice for conducting oneself in arguments, conversation, and courtship — aimed at preserving temper, reputation, and virtue in polite society. Covers how to argue handsomely, when to avoid disputes, and cautions for women's familiarities with men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid disputes as much as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid Disputes as much as possible. To appear easie and well-bred in Conversation, you may assure your self that it requires more Wit, as well as more good Humour, to improve than to contradict the Notions of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer improving another's notions over contradicting them; avoiding disputes is itself a mark of good breeding and wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give reasons with coolness and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are at any time obliged to enter on an Argument, give your Reasons with the utmost Coolness and Modesty, two Things which scarce ever fail of making an Impression on the Hearers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooling, modest presentation of arguments tends to persuade and make a favourable impression; it is recommended whenever one must argue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dogmatism and outward self-importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Be neither Dogmatical, nor shew either by your Actions or Words, that you are full of your self; all will the more heartily rejoice at your Victory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility increases the acceptability of your views and reduces hostility; do not display arrogance or certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retreat gracefully when shown an error
rubrics_metrics.description: Should you be pinched in your Argument, you may make your Retreat with a very good Grace: You were never positive, and are now glad to be better informed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admit the possibility of being mistaken; framing retreat as being glad to learn preserves reputation and avoids rancour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Socratic method / ask questions rather than assert
rubrics_metrics.description: This has made some approve the Socratical Way of Reasoning, where while you scarce affirm any thing, you can hardly be caught in an Absurdity; and tho' possibly you are endeavouring to bring over another to your Opinion, which is firmly fix'd, you seem only to desire Information from him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Socratic questioning reduces the chance of contradiction and entrapment, and can be an effective, modest way to attempt persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep your temper; do not be angry with those who differ
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing can be more unjust or ridiculous, than to be angry with another because he is not of your Opinion... you cannot make a more false Step, or give your Antagonists a greater Advantage over you, than by falling into a Passion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember differences of interest, education, and means; ask yourself how you might think under their biases. Anger weakens your position and gives advantage to opponents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reproach those who fail to apprehend your reasons; pity rather than anger
rubrics_metrics.description: It is yet more absurd to be angry with a Man because he does not apprehend the Force of your Reasons, or gives weak ones of his own... he is certainly in all respects an Object of your Pity, rather than Anger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ignorance or misunderstanding with compassion; anger is counterproductive, especially if you argue partly for reputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Among equals, anger is unvalued and self-destructive
rubrics_metrics.description: That among your Equals no one values your Anger, which only preys upon its Master; and perhaps you may find it not very consistent either with Prudence or your Ease, to punish your self whenever you meet with a Fool or a Knave.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anger harms the angry person more than others; avoid punishing yourself emotionally over others' follies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek information and truth as the true end of argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If you propose to your self the true End of Argument, which is Information, it may be a seasonable Check to your Passion; for if you search purely after Truth, 'twill be almost indifferent to you where you find it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orient arguments toward discovering truth rather than merely winning; this attitude tempers passion and encourages impartiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the role of impartial moderator for esteem
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing procures a Man more Esteem and less Envy from the whole Company, than if he chooses the Part of Moderator, without engaging directly on either Side in a Dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting as moderator lets one sift matters, display judgement, and compliment both sides — it raises esteem and reduces envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: When victorious, do not rub it in
rubrics_metrics.description: When you have gained a Victory, do not push it too far; 'tis sufficient to let the Company and your Adversary see 'tis in your Power, but that you are too generous to make use of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display restraint after winning an argument — demonstrate power but show generosity by not humiliating the opponent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mistake 'salamander' licence for ordinary prudence (women's conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a Species of Women, whom I shall distinguish by the Name of Salamanders... The Salamander knows no Distinction of Sex... She admits a Male Visitant to her Bed-side, plays with him... and is extreamly Scandalized at the unreasonableness of an Husband, or the severity of a Parent, that would debar the Sex from such innocent Liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category is described as an exceptional, almost mythical type; advice that follows is explicitly not for such women but for women 'made of Flesh and Blood' who are subject to frailties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid temptations and opportunities (advice to most women)
rubrics_metrics.description: As for this Part of the fair Sex who are not of the Salamander Kind, I would most earnestly advise them to observe a quite different Conduct in their Behaviour; and to avoid as much as possible what Religion calls Temptations, and the World Opportunities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve virtue by eschewing familiarities and situations that may lead gradually from innocent freedoms to ruin and infamy; shun the first approaches of those who might lead into 'labyrinths of Guilt and Misery.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Distrust excessive familiarity with male companions
rubrics_metrics.description: I exhort the Female Sex... to avoid as much as possible what Religion calls Temptations... Did they but know how many Thousands of their Sex have been gradually betrayed from innocent Freedoms to Ruin and Infamy; and how many Millions of ours have begun with Flatteries, Protestations and Endearments, but ended with Reproaches, Perjury, and Perfidiousness; they would shun like Death the very first Approaches of one that might lead them into inextricable Labyrinths of Guilt and Misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative and the anecdote of the Castilian and his wife illustrate the practical risk: familiarity can be used by opportunistic lovers/renegades to seduce, betray, and ruin reputations and fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust not a man (counsel drawn from dramatic quotation)
rubrics_metrics.description: I must so far give up the Cause of the Male World, as to exhort the Female Sex in the Language of Chamont in the Orphan: 'Trust not a Man, we are by Nature False, Dissembling, Subtle, Cruel, and Unconstant: When a Man talks of Love, with Caution trust him: But if he Swears, he'll certainly deceive thee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A cautionary maxim recommending scepticism toward men's professions of love; useful as a heuristic to avoid imprudent attachments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer a grateful, virtuous wife to being an abandoned mistress
rubrics_metrics.description: From the letter of 'Statira' to 'Oroondates': if you make me your Wife, you may promise your self all the Obedience and Tenderness... Whatever Compliances from an easie Temper... Whatever Consolations from a sincere Friendship... In the other Marriage you will live in a constant Comparison of Benefits, I to the Fortune to which you introduced me. The Commerce between you two will eternally have the Air of a Bargain, between us of a Friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument to men: marriage with a virtuous, grateful woman yields lasting companionship, gratitude, and domestic contentment, whereas temporary pleasures as a mistress lead to shame, solitude, guilt, and the 'bargain'-like commerce of mercenary marriages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not entrust critical affairs or funds to unreliable intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrated by the Castilian story: the husband entrusts the ransom-money to a 'Renegado' or intermediary who betrays his wife and absconds with the money, resulting in the husband's ruin and death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical caution: entrusting money or negotiations to unscrupulous third parties (or overly familiar companions) risks betrayal; avoid unnecessary reliance on doubtful agents.
